newsitem.title: USA: AT&T had doubts on Walter's as leader-director.
newsitem.headline: AT&T had doubts on Walter's as leader-director.

text.p: AT&T Corp's board opted not to elect President and Chief Operating Officer John Walter as AT&T chief executive based on doubts about his ability to lead the company, a member of the AT&T board said on Wednesday.

In a conference call with reporters late Wednesday afternoon, Walter Elisha, said the decision to delay Walter's elevation as chief executive, replacing Robert Allen, the current chief executive, came after months of consideration.

Walter chose to resign Wednesday morning from AT&T after the eight independent directors on AT&T 11-member board voted Tuesday evening not to elect him as chief executive on its original timetable, Elisha said.
Elisha is chairman and chief executive of textile firm Springs Industries Inc, a board member of AT&T, and a spokesman for AT&T's eight independent directors.

"It may well have been that we erred in bringing him in the first place," Elisha said in response to a reporter's question about the decision to hire Walter as the heir apparent to Allen last November.

"We became increasingly concerned that this was going to work," he said, referring to a succession plan under which Walter was due to be elected chief executive in January 1998, when Allen planned to step aside.
Robert Allen has agreed to remain as chairman and chief executive for an open-ended period while a search is conducted for a replacement as chief executive, the director said.
Elisha said the board's action was taken as a result of discussion among the eight independent directors on AT&T's board at meetings held Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.
The eight directors voted unamiously not to elect Walter according to the original January timeline at the Tuesday night meeting, the board member said.

Walter resigned after the board made clear it was not prepared to elect him immediately at a meeting Wednesday morning. Robert Allen took part in the initial part of the Tuesday meeting, but was not present during the discussions leading to the vote. Allen had recommended to the board that they not elect Walter to become chief executive in January.
The board member said Allen had expressed reservations at monthly meetings with board members since April.
"I don't view the hiring of Mr. Walter as a mistake," Elisha said, responding to a reporter's question. "You're using 20/20 hindsight.
"No one is chief executive until he is elected chief executive."
Asked to defend the hefty severance package Walter will receive after less than nine months on the job, Elisha pointed to other executives at top companies that are paid similarly.
He mentioned International Business Machines Corp's Louis Gerstner, Eastman Kodak Co's George Fischer and AT&T's Allen.
"I think John's name would be on the final list of 10 candiates but there are other strong internal candidates," Elisha said. "I am simply not precluding anybody."
AT&T's boardroom coup follows a year of management turmoil, which reflects a larger confusion about strategic direction at the company, analysts said.

AT&T faces falling market share in its core long-distance business and the need to make hefty new investments to enter new markets, especially in the local service business, as regulators seek to open the industry to wider competition.

"This guy walked into a minefield," Forrester Research analyst David Goodtree said, listing what he labelled as the "sicknesses" ailing the nation's largest long-distance company -- well before Walter even arrived on the scene.
"Earnings were falling, market share was sliding, management needed a cleaning of house and captial expenses were going through the roof and no one knew what was going on," the analyst said.
"Walter couldn't win," Goodtree said. "It doesn't matter how great he was."
Walter joins a flood of departing AT&T executives, including Jerry Salemme, head of government regulatory affairs, the heads of AT&T's international operations and wireless business.

Walter himself was responsible for firing the company's former consumer long-distance chief, Joe Nacchio, who left to join Qwest Communicatios International Inc and is rumored to have pushed aside Ron Ponder as chief information officer.
The beginning of the exodous is pegged to the departure of Alex Mandl last August to become chief executive of a wireless start-up now known as Teligent.
Mandl had served as president and chief operating officer and was considered by many analysts as Allen's heir apparent.
"What is wrong with this picture?" Goodtree asked.
